faq.q: What is inside a light switch?
faq.a: A light switch hides a pair of metal contacts and a springy rocker. When you flick it, a spring snaps the contacts together or apart quickly, so the gap opens cleanly.
asks: How does a light switch work inside?

faq.q: Why can't electricity jump across the gap?
faq.a: Air is an insulator because its electrons are held tightly by their atoms. At household voltage a gap of a few millimetres is far too wide for a spark to cross, so the flow simply stops.
asks: Why doesn't the current cross the air?

faq.q: Does the switch stop the electricity everywhere?
faq.a: Yes. Current flows round the whole loop at the same time, so breaking it at one point stops it everywhere, even in the wire on the far side of the bulb.
asks: Does it matter where the switch is in the loop?

faq.q: Why does a switch snap instead of moving slowly?
faq.a: If the contacts parted slowly, a small spark could jump and burn them. A spring makes them snap apart fast, so any spark is tiny and the switch lasts for years.

faq.q: Which wire is the light switch in?
faq.a: Electricians put the switch in the live wire. Then, when it is off, the bulb holder is cut off from the high voltage, which makes changing a bulb safer.
asks: Why is the switch in the live wire?

facts: Household light switches are wired into the live wire, not the neutral.
Dry air needs roughly 3 million volts per metre before a spark can jump through it.
